newsitem.title: USA: US Democrat lawmakers urge Fed not to raise rates.
newsitem.headline: US Democrat lawmakers urge Fed not to raise rates.

text.p: A group of Democrat lawmakers urged the Federal Reserve Friday not to raise interest rates at its policy-making meeting next month.
"The Federal Reserve shouldn't further raise interest rates," House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri said.
He said the Fed needed to adopt a new approach. "They need to help promote growth and a rising standard of living rather than view prosperity as a threat to our economy," Gephardt said.
The lawmakers released a letter sent to Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan that said "now is not the time to further raise interest rates and put economic growth and opportunity at risk."
The letter was signed by 62 Democrats, one Republican, Rep. Jim Bunning of Kentucky, and one Independent, Rep. Bernard Sanders of Vermont.

The Fed last raised interest rates on March 25, when short-term rates were increased a quarter of a percentage point. The next meeting of the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee is May 20.
Sen. Tom Harkin, an Iowa Democrat, said he was going to take a "long, hard look" at President Clinton's nominees to two vacancies on the Fed Board.
Harkin, who has long been a critic of the Fed, helped hold up Greenspan's renomination to another term as Fed chairman last year. Greenspan was eventually confirmed.
Clinton plans to name Roger Ferguson, a partner with consulting firm McKinsey & Co Inc, and Edward Gramlich, a University of Michigan economist, to fill the vacancies.
Harkin said he has instructed his staff to get economic writings done by the two expected nominees.
"The early indications are we're going to have more of the same from these two nominees," Harkin said. "I don't want to prejudge them, but ... early indications are they're just cookie cutters."
"I'm not about to rubber-stamp anybody," Harkin said. He added that he would seek to have extensive debate on the Senate floor on the two Fed nominees, "maybe even more so than on Mr. Greenspan."
Harkin's demand for floor time on Greenspan's nomination last year held up that nomination for weeks.
